title: Why We're Teaching Reading Comprehension In A Way That Doesn't Work
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that after the phonics debate, the larger scandal in reading instruction is how comprehension is taught and how teachers are trained to teach it. She traces the problem to the 2001 National Reading Panel, whose endorsement of comprehension strategies overlooked the stronger evidence that background knowledge of the topic is the biggest factor in understanding a text, as in the well-known baseball experiment. Typical lessons, she says, foreground a strategy or skill on easy texts chosen without regard to topic, repeated for years although benefits fade after about two weeks, while leveled reading has no evidence behind it and does little to build knowledge. She also challenges the belief that children must learn to read before they read to learn, which has squeezed history, science and the arts out of elementary schools, and notes that Common Core's nonfiction push has often just added new skills to drill. Her constructive point is that knowledge-building curricula now exist in places like Baltimore, Detroit and Louisiana, and that teachers can learn to provide both decoding skills and the knowledge that unlocks meaning.
points: Wexler's central claim is that knowledge of the topic, not mastery of strategies, is the most important driver of reading comprehension, and that strategies depend on prior knowledge to work at all.

Strategy instruction is both over-taught and mis-taught: the research-backed approach puts a difficult text in the foreground, whereas typical lessons put the skill first and pick simple texts to fit it.
Leveled reading and the learn-to-read-then-read-to-learn assumption both delay knowledge building, which widens the gap between children who gain knowledge outside school and those who do not.
Common Core's call for more nonfiction backfired where teachers simply added nonfiction skills, since nonfiction presumes more background knowledge than fiction.
She sees a way forward in knowledge-rich elementary curricula, adopted in Baltimore and Detroit, and in teachers learning on the job what their training omitted.
quotes: What the report failed to mention was the strong evidence showing that the most important factor in comprehension isn’t mastering strategies: it’s how much knowledge a reader has of the topic. In one well-known experiment, students who scored poorly on a reading test but knew a lot about baseball outperformed “good readers” who knew little about baseball—when the reading passage was about baseball.

But most of the things teachers spend hours on every week were never endorsed by the National Reading Panel and have little or no data behind them. As reading expert Tim Shanahan has observed, teaching such “skills” is like pushing the elevator button twice: it might make you feel better, but it won’t make the elevator come any faster.

Rather than putting a difficult text in the foreground and modeling whatever strategies might help students extract its meaning, teachers put a strategy in the foreground and choose simple texts that lend themselves to demonstrating it, without regard to their topics. And they teach comprehension day after day, year after year—sometimes through high school. But studies have shown that after only two weeks of strategy instruction, students stop getting benefits.

But there’s no evidence that this system of leveled reading boosts comprehension, and studies have found that kids can learn more from a text above their supposed level—if a teacher helps them understand it. Plus, leveled reading does little to build knowledge, a process that generally requires staying on the same topic for at least a couple of weeks.

But the idea that kids don't need to acquire knowledge until after they’ve learned to read ignores the fact that gaining knowledge is part of learning to read—or learning to understand what you read. Even while they’re learning to decode, children need to listen to adults reading aloud from sophisticated, knowledge-rich text.

It’s one thing to make an inference about a fictional character’s thoughts, based on your knowledge of human nature. It’s quite another to make an inference about, say, Brazil if you’ve never even heard of the place.

Just a few years ago, there were no elementary literacy curricula designed to build students’ knowledge. Now there are several—and two large urban districts, Baltimore and Detroit, have each started implementing one, while the state of Louisiana has been encouraging their adoption.
